source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs acting as a flight assistant barely improve across five rounds of evidence. A Bayesian assistant keeps improving. Most LLMs plateau after round 1.
numbers: Task: 5 rounds, 624 simulated users; models Gemma 2 9B/27B, Llama 3 8B/70B, Qwen 2.5 7B/32B, GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro. Bayesian Assistant final-round accuracy about 80%; small LLMs near 37% (random level) in both round 1 and round 5.
quote: LLMs' performance often plateaus after a single interaction, pointing to a limited ability to adapt to new information.
limits: One synthetic preference-learning task; numbers read from figure text, so approximate.
agent_relevance: Evidence of weak S5 revise: a model may answer well once but not accumulate evidence over turns. Test our scaffold on multi-round updating, not only single answers.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Fine-tuning on a Bayesian assistant's outputs (Bayesian teaching) taught models to keep updating, beat training on always-correct answers (oracle teaching), and generalised to hotel and web-shopping tasks.
numbers: Fine-tuned models agree with the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time (original and oracle-tuned lower); gains significant at p<0.001, 3 seeds. Web-shopping gap between Bayesian and oracle teaching is smaller than in flights.
limits: Needs weight training; our agent cannot fine-tune. Shows the skill is learnable from examples of gradual updates, not only from correct answers.
agent_relevance: A scaffold could show worked examples of graded updates (not just correct end answers) as in-context demonstrations. Untested here.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Simple prompting fixes did not help: chain-of-thought, numeric formatting, 30 rounds instead of 5, and base models all left updating poor. Giving the model the exact Bayesian posterior in text improved belief-based accuracy.
numbers: Appendix C.1 / Fig 9. Humans (48 of the 624 users) improved from round 1 to 5 (p=0.002), beat small LLMs, and fell short of the Bayesian assistant like all models.
limits: Direct-prediction accuracy did not improve with the supplied posterior in the passage read (text partly cut). Human sample small.
agent_relevance: Do not count on 'think step by step' for S5. Separating inference of the belief state from using it may matter; an external explicit belief record is worth testing.

source: Gupta et al. (2025) Enough Coin Flips Can Make LLMs Act Bayesian
finding: In a biased-coin task, LLMs broadly follow Bayesian posterior updates in context. Errors come mainly from miscalibrated priors, not from wrong update steps. In-context evidence outweighs explicit bias instructions.
numbers: Open models (Gemma-2 and others, 70M to 12B range incl. Pythia, Phi-3, Llama 3.1). Four findings in the abstract: biased priors, evidence beats instruction, Bayesian-like updates, attention magnitude negligible.
quote: LLMs update their priors in a Bayesian manner
limits: Toy Bernoulli task with many demonstrations; contrasts with Qiu where real preference inference fails. Open models only.
agent_relevance: Updating on clean, repeated, simple evidence may be fine; failure is in the prior and in complex or sparse evidence. Make the agent state its prior explicitly before revising.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of LLM Reasoning (Belief-R)
finding: On Belief-R, 30 language models mostly fail to retract a conclusion when a new premise defeats it. Most open models score about 0% on the belief-update subset. The best reach at most about 50% on the combined BREU score.
numbers: Llama-3 70B Instruct: belief-update accuracy 10.99%, belief-maintain 92.09% (BREU 51.5%). GPT-4 Turbo: BU 19.65%, BM 82.69%. Basic logical inference accuracy was above 75% for models over 6B.
limits: Logic-puzzle belief revision (modus ponens/tollens), not probabilistic forecasting. Crowd-annotated; 100 samples checked.
agent_relevance: S5 should carry an explicit test: does the new fact defeat an earlier conclusion? Models default to keeping the old answer.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of LLM Reasoning (Belief-R)
finding: There is a trade-off. Models that update more also wrongly update when they should keep their belief. Chain-of-thought and plan-and-solve prompting did not help; harder tasks (modus tollens, abstract mental-state premises) made revision worse.
numbers: Mixtral 8x22B direct prompting BU 35.4%, BM 36.6%; Command R+ plan-and-solve BU 44.0%, BM 53.1%. Prompting changes BREU by about 1 point.
limits: Single-step revisions only.
agent_relevance: Any scaffold that forces more updating must be scored on keep-the-belief items too, or it will only inflate flip rates.

source: Filbry, Melo and Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
finding: Non-reasoning LLMs violate Bayes' rule when updating in context. Probability-axiom violations are common across separate conversations but fall sharply inside one dialogue.
numbers: Cross-conversation violation rates above 50% of 30 scenarios for almost all model-axiom pairs; within one dialogue about 10% for Gemini and 1 of 30 for Gemma. Wrong updates cut final success by at least 30% versus an oracle; near 0% on 20Q for weaker models.
limits: Models: Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemma 4 31B, Qwen 2.5 32B. Synthetic environments (20Q, ProteinWorld). Preprint Oct 2026.
agent_relevance: Keep earlier probability judgments visible in the same context; coherence comes from access to prior judgments. Supports an external belief ledger in S5.

source: Filbry, Melo and Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
finding: Reasoning mode and code execution close most of the gap: reasoning models reach KL near 0 on the easy posterior task, and Gemini 2.5 Pro with Python approximates an intractable posterior.
numbers: Gemma-4-31B-it matches the oracle across ProteinWorld-simple; consistent for up to 10 experiments on 20Q. Without code, ProteinWorld-hard gave hallucinated simulation output; with code KL and gap are near 0.
limits: Remaining errors with reasoning were numerical slips, not conceptual. Hard case needed tools. Tasks are closed-form or simulable.
agent_relevance: S5 should call a calculator or code for the update step when likelihoods are explicit, and verify arithmetic.

source: Li et al. (2026) Same Answer, Different Future: Matched Predictions Do Not Imply Matched Belief Updating in Language Models
finding: Two ways of putting a belief into a model can give the same current prediction but different resistance to new evidence. The effective weight of a stated summary scales weakly with its stated observation count.
numbers: Three open models, four textual routes and two activation interventions in a Bernoulli task; effective weights differ across routes, and elicitation questions change inferred weights by orders of magnitude. A steering intervention loses most of its effect after later evidence.
limits: Open models, toy task; abstract, introduction and some result fragments read. Preprint Nov 2026.
agent_relevance: If our agent summarises earlier evidence into a note, the model may give that summary too little weight versus raw observations. Keep raw evidence counts visible, not just a stated rate.

source: Shapira, Cheng and Orgad (2026) Is Sycophancy a Form of In-Context Updating?
finding: Deference to a user's false claim looks like a general in-context updating process. Models also update on claims attributed to a credible source, and mitigations that cut sycophancy also cut useful updating.
numbers: Across models the two adoption rates co-vary. Opus 5 adopted the user's suggestion 21% of the time versus Sonnet 5 78%, but adopted a credible source's suggestion only 27% versus 98%, including when revision was warranted.
limits: Preprint Oct 2026; model names as given in the paper; multiple-choice style items.
agent_relevance: Trade-off for S5: anti-sycophancy that blocks all updating hurts. Weight new evidence by source reliability, not by who said it.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval-augmented GPT-4 forecasting system nears the crowd on questions published after its cutoff but does not beat it overall.
numbers: Test set: questions after 1 Jun 2023, five platforms. Brier .179 vs crowd .149; accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Averaging with the crowd (crowd weight 4x) gives .146 vs .149.
limits: Crowd aggregate still better overall. Retrieval at fixed dates, not a live updating agent.
agent_relevance: Reference point for how far an evidence-reading LLM is from human crowds; judge S5 gains on Brier, not accuracy.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: The system beat the crowd on early retrieval dates and when the crowd was uncertain, but lagged late in a question's life and where the crowd was confident. The authors say it hedges even as evidence becomes decisive.
numbers: Crowd between .3 and .7: system Brier .199 vs crowd .246. Where crowd is within .05 of 0 or 1: accuracy 7% higher but Brier worse by .04. Selective setting meeting all three conditions: .240 vs crowd .247 on 22% of forecasts / 43% of questions. With at least 5 relevant articles the system improves and passes the crowd.
quote: tendency to hedge predictions due to its safety training
limits: Selection conditions were derived on validation data; the safety-training explanation is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Direct sign of under-updating toward certainty as evidence arrives. S5 needs an explicit rule to move away from 0.5 when evidence is decisive.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Ablations: retrieval and a fine-tuned reasoning model each help. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 and base GPT-4 are close. No retrieval plus no fine-tuned reasoning is worst.
numbers: Brier: full .179, fine-tuned GPT-3.5 .182, base GPT-4 .181, no IR .183, weaker rows .186 and .206, against crowd .146 (SE about .002). Calibration error mostly underconfidence at the extremes.
limits: Standard errors about .002-.003, so small gaps are noise.
agent_relevance: Evidence retrieval is worth up to about .02 Brier; the reasoning step is worth a similar amount.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs (median) matched a human crowd on 31 binary questions. Models showed an acquiescence bias, with mean forecasts above 50% though outcomes were near even.
numbers: Study 1: 12 LLMs vs 925 human forecasters, 31 questions; LLM crowd Brier M=0.20 (SD .12) vs human M=0.19 (SD .19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.85.
limits: Small question set; equivalence shown only at medium effect-size bounds.
agent_relevance: Aggregate several independent drafts before S5; a single draft leans positive.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Study 2: showing GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median made them update, with moves proportional to the gap. But averaging the model's first forecast with the human median beat the model's own update.
numbers: 186 primary and 186 updated forecasts. GPT-4 Brier .17 to .14 (p=.003); Claude 2 .22 to .15 (p<.001). Update size correlates with initial gap r=.88 (GPT-4), r=.87 (Claude 2). Simple average scored .13 and .14, better than the updates (t(92)=2.58 p=.011; t(92)=3.53 p=.001). Prediction intervals narrowed.
limits: Social-information updating, not evidence updating; same 31 questions.
agent_relevance: Models update in the right direction and proportion, but not enough. Moving toward the midpoint with strong outside information beats letting the model judge alone.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
finding: Human forecasters who could consult an LLM assistant were more accurate than a control with a weak assistant, even when the assistant was deliberately overconfident and ignored base rates.
numbers: N=991, six questions, preregistered. Accuracy gains 24% to 28% vs control. Without one outlier item, 41% for the superforecasting assistant vs 29% for the noisy one.
limits: Data did not consistently support benefit to low-skill forecasters; one outlier item drove part of the effect.
agent_relevance: Humans gain from advice they can revise on; keep a revision step even when an advisor is noisy.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: On a dynamic benchmark, superforecasters beat the general public and the best LLM. LLM scores track model strength.
numbers: 39 superforecasters, mean Brier 0.096 vs public 0.121 (p<0.001) vs Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122 on a 200-question subset. Linear fits project LLM parity with superforecasters near Arena score 1406 or training compute near 6.5e26 FLOP, with wide intervals.
limits: Extrapolation is uncertain; benchmark snapshot from 2024.
agent_relevance: The gap to superforecasters was real in 2024; the next lines show it closing with search, aggregation and extremizing.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report
finding: An agentic search plus supervisor plus Platt-scaling system is statistically indistinguishable from superforecasters on ForecastBench.
numbers: Brier: FB-Market .0753 vs superforecasters .0740 vs public .1035; FB-7-21 .1076 vs .1110 vs .1451; MarketLiquid .1258 vs market price .1106 (worse). Ensemble with market beats market alone.
limits: Vendor report, not peer reviewed; underperforms liquid market prices.
agent_relevance: A tuned pipeline can reach expert level; its parts (search, reconcile, extremize) map onto S5.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report
finding: LLMs hedge toward 0.5, attributed to RLHF. Statistical extremising (Platt scaling) corrects it. Agentic search beats plain search; a supervisor that reconciles forecasts beats plain averaging.
numbers: No search 0.1230; agentic Search-A 0.1140; non-agentic Search-A 0.1174. Agentic supervisor 0.1125 vs non-agentic supervisor 0.1168. Platt scaling on the mean gave lowest Brier and matched superforecasters.
quote: LLMs have an annoying bias ... which makes them hedge toward 0.5 when making predictions
limits: Platt coefficient tuned on the benchmark; the hedge explanation is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Add an anti-hedge check to S5: after revising, ask whether the stance is more moderate than the evidence supports.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Logical consistency of a forecaster across related questions correlates with its later Brier score. Conditional-probability checks correlate most.
numbers: Cond check r=0.92 (arbitrage) and 0.87 (frequentist) on scraped questions; aggregated 0.62 / 0.85. ExpEvidence (law of total probability, a check on coherent updating) 0.20 / 0.77. Negation, Or and ExpEvidence correlated weakly or negatively on the NewsAPI set. Also a 3,000-check long-horizon benchmark resolving in 2028.
limits: Correlation across forecasters of mixed strength; part is just better models being both more consistent and more accurate.
agent_relevance: Cheap test for S5: ask for P(A), P(A given B), P(A given not B) and P(B) and check they cohere.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Forcing consistency does not fix forecasting. An ArbitrageForecaster that patches outputs raised consistency on the checks it trained on but did not generalise to held-out checks and did not improve Brier.
numbers: Consistency gains largest for Negation, then Paraphrase, lowest for ExpEvidence; recursive depth helped only on the trained check.
limits: Few setups, gpt-4o-mini base, preliminary.
agent_relevance: Consistency is a diagnostic, not a cure. Do not tune S5 only to pass consistency checks.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) The psychology of intelligence analysis: drivers of prediction accuracy in world politics
finding: In the IARPA tournament, frequency of belief updating was among the behavioural predictors of accuracy, with deliberation time, intelligence, knowledge and open-mindedness. Skill was consistent over time.
numbers: More than 150,000 forecasts, 743 participants, 199 events over 2 years.
limits: Only the abstract (Europe PMC record) was read; no effect sizes seen. Updating link is correlational.
agent_relevance: Frequent revising marks good forecasters; the human basis for S5.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Randomised training, teaming and tracking each improved calibration and resolution in the 2-year tournament.
numbers: Abstract reports gains in both calibration and resolution; elite-team tracking used the top 2% from Year 1.
limits: Abstract only; effect sizes not seen here. The next line is a reanalysis that disputes it.
agent_relevance: Training in probabilities, reference classes and averaging is the intervention family closest to our scaffold.

source: Rethinking the Role of Teams and Training in Geopolitical Forecasting: The Effect of Uncontrolled Method Variance on Statistical Conclusions (2025, Psychological Science)
finding: A reanalysis of the same tournament with item response theory found that once extraneous variables were controlled, the effects of teaming and training were substantially reduced, eliminated, or in some models reversed.
numbers: Best-fit models over the first 2 years included extraneous variables. Latent traits tied to strategic responding separated superforecasters from others.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC). Full effect sizes not seen. A reanalysis of existing data, not a new experiment.
agent_relevance: Treat training effect sizes in forecasting as less settled. Do not assume a prompt of the same kind transfers without measurement.

source: Atanasov, Witkowski, Ungar, Mellers and Tetlock (2020) Small steps to accuracy: Incremental belief updaters are better forecasters. OBHDP 160, 19-35
finding: Claim as cited by others: forecasters who update often in small increments are more accurate. The primary text was not reachable (HTTP 403 and redirects).
numbers: No numbers obtained. Two open-access reviews read this session cite it as showing frequent incremental updating is among the best predictors of accuracy.
limits: Not opened. Another pass should extract N, Brier effects and how much of the superforecaster advantage updating explains.
agent_relevance: Core S5 evidence for small steps. Check against the full paper before quoting.

source: Himmelstein, Budescu and colleagues (2024) Human and Algorithmic Predictions in Geopolitical Forecasting, Perspectives on Psychological Science
finding: Review of the tournament. Aggregates weighted toward recent forecasts (forecasters who updated were more likely to have better information), plus track-record weights and extremising. Best individual predictors include frequent incremental updating.
numbers: Cites Atanasov et al. 2020 (updating), Friedman et al. 2017 (granular use of the probability scale), Mellers et al. 2017 (coherence). Extremising depends on information overlap among forecasters.
limits: Review; no new data on updating itself.
agent_relevance: Supports recency weighting and extremising: late revisions carry more information, and a pooled view should be pushed away from 0.5.

source: Tetlock, Mellers, Rohrbaugh and Chen (2014) Judging political judgment, PNAS
finding: Dispute over whether experts are well calibrated: earlier poor results were concentrated in long-range forecasts, whereas the compared intelligence forecasts were short-term; tournaments add training and accountability.
numbers: In the Mandel and Barnes data, 59% of questions were under 6 months and 96% under a year; Brier scores of 0 or 0.01 over half the time.
limits: No direct belief-updating data; read through a page summary that may omit details.
agent_relevance: Horizon matters. Do not generalise small-step updating results from short-horizon questions to long-horizon ones.

source: Tetlock (2005) Expert Political Judgment
finding: Long-run study of expert forecasters: experts were often little better than simple baselines and foxes beat hedgehogs. Belief-system defences made experts slow to update on disconfirming outcomes.
numbers: About 284 experts and about 28,000 predictions over roughly 20 years (from memory, not verified this session).
limits: Not opened. Numbers from memory.
agent_relevance: Origin of the concern that strong priors block revision. Verify numbers before quoting.

source: Edwards (1968) Conservatism in human information processing
finding: Classic finding that people revise probabilities less than Bayes' rule requires when evidence arrives (conservatism).
numbers: No numbers obtained.
limits: Not opened. Competing account: some studies find overreaction to vivid evidence; direction depends on diagnosticity.
agent_relevance: Prior art for the LLM plateau result in Qiu: weak updating is old in humans too.

source: Soll and Larrick (2009) Strategies for revising judgment: How (and how well) people use others' opinions
finding: People tend to under-weight others' opinions and keep their own; simple averaging would improve them. Seen only as a reference entry in the Himmelstein review text.
numbers: No numbers obtained.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Schoenegger Study 2: revision toward outside information falls short of simple averaging.
